stances.claim: The 1987 Philippine Constitution safeguards religious worship more expansively than the US First Amendment: Article III Section 5 includes both the establishment and free-exercise clauses but goes beyond them by expressly guaranteeing the 'free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference,' and prohibiting any 'religious test... for the exercise of civil or political rights.'

Voluntary recitation of the SC's 2001 Centennial Prayer for the Courts at every court session, and the allowance of Catholic Masses (and other religious rituals) in the Halls of Justice under In Re: Valenzuela (March 7, 2017, SC en banc, one dissent), does NOT violate the separation of church and state.

Philippine separation of church and state requires only that the government be 'benevolently neutral' in the 'competition... amongst different religious denominations' -- meaning Congress cannot appropriate, and the President cannot spend, public funds to build a basilica for one denomination, promote one dogma to the detriment of others, pay clergy salaries for strictly religious duties, or use religion as a work prerequisite.

Personal-thesis disclosure: 'the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic. In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God. At bottom, while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God.'

The American right to keep and bear arms -- born of the 1775-1783 independence struggle and codified in the Second Amendment -- has been progressively enlarged by Scotus conservatives via the Fourteenth Amendment's due-process and equal-protection clauses, extending coverage from the 'ancient militia' to all American citizens, making it 'difficult [for states] to regulate and control gun ownership and use' despite recent shootings.

Our Constitution does not grant a similar right to keep and bear arms; Philippine Congress has passed stringent laws on gun ownership and use -- a deliberate constitutional-statutory contrast with the American framework.

notable_anecdotes: The 2001 Centennial Prayer for the Courts preserved verbatim -- 'Almighty God, we stand in Your holy presence as our Supreme Judge. We humbly beseech You to bless and inspire us so that what we think, say, and do will be in accordance with your will... so that we can be effective channels of truth, justice, and peace... guide us in the path of righteousness for the fulfillment of your greater glory. Amen.' -- used as the column's most distinctive Philippine-institutional artifact illustrating state-faith intersection without church-state breach.

The trans-charter Preamble comparison: 1987 ('imploring the aid of Almighty God'), 1973 and 1935 ('imploring the aid of Divine Providence') as evidence of unbroken Philippine constitutional theism, contrasted with the US Constitution's silence (offset by the 'In God We Trust' currency motto).

CJ's signature paradox formulation -- 'while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God' -- a quotable theological-civic distinction that crystallizes Philippine benevolent-neutrality doctrine.

In Re: Valenzuela (March 7, 2017) en banc 'with one dissent' permitting Catholic Masses and other religious rituals in Halls of Justice -- preserved as the boldest concrete extension of benevolent-neutrality reasoning into court premises.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing from his previous Monday column on the three June 2022 Scotus 6-3 decisions (abortion, religious worship, right to bear arms), Panganiban turns to the second and third rulings and contrasts US with Philippine treatment of these rights. He argues that the 1987 Philippine Constitution safeguards religious worship more expansively than the US First Amendment: Article III Section 5 includes both the establishment and free-exercise clauses but goes beyond them by guaranteeing 'free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession and worship, without discrimination or preference' and prohibiting any 'religious test... for the exercise of civil or political rights.' Across three Philippine charters (1987, 1973, 1935), the Preamble has always invoked Almighty God or Divine Providence -- unlike the US Constitution, though the US Congress adopted 'In God We Trust' as currency motto. He recounts the SC's 2001 Centennial Prayer for the Courts (preserved verbatim) recited at every court session and the bolder extension in In Re: Valenzuela (March 7, 2017, SC en banc, one dissent) permitting Catholic Masses and other religious rituals in Halls of Justice -- neither violates separation of church and state because that doctrine requires only 'benevolent neutrality' in the 'competition... amongst different religious denominations,' meaning the government cannot fund a basilica, promote one dogma, pay clergy salaries, or impose a religious work prerequisite. He offers his signature paradox: 'the Philippines is theist, not atheist, not even agnostic. In fact, it is monotheist; it worships one God. At bottom, while there is separation of church and state, there is no separation of the state from God.' On the American right to keep and bear arms -- anchored in the Second Amendment ('A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear arms, shall not be infringed') and born of the 1775-1783 independence struggle -- he diagnoses doctrinal evolution: Scotus conservatives have progressively enlarged its coverage from the 'ancient militia' to all American citizens via the Fourteenth Amendment's due-process and equal-protection clauses, making it 'difficult [for states] to regulate and control gun ownership' despite recent US shootings. The Philippine Constitution grants no similar right, and Congress has passed stringent gun-ownership laws -- a deliberate constitutional-statutory contrast.
